draft_text:
In August 1944, a quarter of a million soldiers landed on the beaches of Provence. Most of them were African. They fought through southern France, pushed the Wehrmacht northward, and helped end Nazi occupation. Then, for the better part of eighty years, Europe forgot them. Not forgot — that implies an accident. This was something more deliberate: a sustained, structural act of erasure, the kind that requires effort to maintain across decades of textbooks, monuments, and national mythologies. The exhibition opening at Haus der Kulturen der Welt on 21 March, Tirailleurs: Trials and Tribulations — From Cannon Fodder to Avant-Garde, is an attempt to reverse that current.

The timing is not incidental. In August 2024, Emmanuel Macron hosted a ceremony marking the 80th anniversary of the Provence landings — Operation Dragoon, the less famous sibling of D-Day. African heads of state were invited. Le Monde reported on the colonial soldiers who "came from the colonies." The spectacle was, by most accounts, [~a classic commemorative gesture: visible enough to claim credit, thin enough to avoid reckoning|coverage of the anniversary ceremony is largely from French broadsheets — Le Monde, Libération — and tends to note the gap between symbolic recognition and material redress~]. Tirailleurs at HKW picks up where that ceremony's press photos left off, and pushes considerably further.

The project is led by Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung, who has served as artistic director of HKW since 2023 and who, before that, ran the Berlin-based project space SAVVY Contemporary for over a decade. Ndikung's curatorial DNA is rooted in exactly the kind of diasporic, post-colonial, thoroughly transnational thinking this exhibition demands. His Cameroonian heritage places him within the very geography the Tirailleurs were drawn from — West and Central Africa — and his track record suggests he is unlikely to treat the subject as a heritage exercise. The word "avant-garde" in the exhibition's subtitle is not decorative. It is a claim: that these soldiers were not merely victims to be pitied or heroes to be celebrated in bronze, but agents who reshaped the cultural and political conditions of 20th-century Europe. That is a genuinely ambitious thesis, and whether the exhibition can sustain it across three months and thirty-plus artists remains to be seen.

The roster is extensive and multigenerational. Kader Attia, whose work on colonial trauma and the concept of "repair" has been central to contemporary art discourse for over a decade, sits alongside Josèfa Ntjam, whose video work Dislocations (2022) — co-produced with Palais de Tokyo and the Cincinnati Contemporary Arts Center — uses speculative fiction to disrupt linear colonial narratives. Tuấn Andrew Nguyễn contributes an ongoing two-channel video installation, Our Empty Uniforms Marched To The Echoes Of An Invisible, that draws on audio from the Lautarchiv der Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, a phonographic archive whose own history is entangled with colonial-era ethnographic recording. Tiffany Chung presents a newly commissioned embroidered textile that explicitly connects Tirailleurs to Japanese military "comfort women" and colonial worker-soldiers — a move that widens the frame from France's specific amnesia to a global pattern of wartime exploitation and subsequent forgetting. Fourteen of the works are new commissions. The exhibition also incorporates research from five international art spaces and collectives, including Raw Material Company in Dakar and Alice Yard in Port of Spain, which signals that this is not a project content to view colonial military history through a purely European lens.

The film programme deepens the historical register. Ousmane Sembène and Thierno Faty Sow's Camp de Thiaroye (1988) — a searing dramatisation of the 1944 massacre of Tirailleurs by the French army at a transit camp in Senegal — stands as one of the most significant African films ever made about the betrayal of colonial soldiers. Rachid Bouchareb's Indigènes (2006), released in English as Days of Glory, was the film that forced the French government to equalise military pensions for African veterans. Philip Scheffner, a Berlin-based documentarian whose work on Germany's colonial afterlives is meticulous and unsettling, brings a specifically German perspective to a history that Germany has largely treated as someone else's problem. [~The screening programme spans several decades and continents, which is rare for a single exhibition's film component|I'm working from the exhibition's own listings here — independent critical coverage of the full film programme is not yet available, as the show hasn't opened~].

What happens inside HKW's Kongresshalle — that famous shell-shaped Cold War relic designed by Hugh Stubbins for the 1957 Interbau exhibition, originally a gift from the United States to West Berlin — carries its own layer of irony. A building conceived as a symbol of American-led freedom and Western democratic values now houses an exhibition about the African soldiers whose sacrifice made that freedom possible and who were then denied its benefits. The architecture was built as propaganda; the exhibition turns it into a site of counter-memory. Ndikung and co-curator Paz Guevara seem acutely aware of this. The subtitle frames the exhibition as "a common space for celebration and deliberation" — language that insists on both joy and criticality, refusing the earnest solemnity that often deadens institutional engagements with difficult history.

The opening weekend is built to match this ambition. Keynote lectures from David Olusoga, the historian whose work on Black British history and the First World War has done more than almost anyone's to bring colonial military service into mainstream Anglophone consciousness, and Santanu Das, whose scholarship on the sensory and emotional lives of colonial soldiers in wartime is richly textured. Live music from Cheikh Lô — the Senegalese singer whose blend of mbalax, jazz, and Afro-Cuban rhythms has made him one of West Africa's most internationally beloved musicians — and Abel Selaocoe performing with Bantu Ensemble. This is not an opening where you look at art, drink wine, and leave. It is programmed as an event in itself.

The question that hovers over everything is the one that hovers over all institutional post-colonial exhibitions in 2026: does it move anything beyond the walls of the institution? [~Germany's engagement with its own role in the Tirailleur story — not just as France's neighbour but as the country these soldiers helped liberate — remains remarkably thin|critical and scholarly coverage of the specifically German dimension of Tirailleur history is sparse compared to the French-language literature, which is itself far from voluminous~]. The exhibition's stated goal of addressing how "unknown" this history is "especially in Germany today" is honest, but it also reveals the scale of the task. Cultural education programmes will run throughout the exhibition's three-month span, and free entry on Mondays and select Sundays lowers the material barrier. Whether this translates into a broader public conversation or remains within the HKW audience — already primed for this kind of engagement — is the difference between an important exhibition and a transformative one.

Still, the sheer density of what is gathered here — the archival research, the new commissions, the film programme, the live events, the transcontinental collaborative network — suggests something more than a commemorative gesture. Commemoration is what Macron did on a beach in Provence. What Ndikung appears to be attempting at HKW is an argument: that the exclusion of African soldiers from Europe's liberation narrative is not a footnote but a foundational distortion, one that warps how Europe understands its own freedom, its own modernity, its own supposed universalism. The avant-garde referenced in the title is not an art-historical category. It is literal. These soldiers were the advance guard. They went first. And then they were written out of the story that their bodies made possible.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine argument and real edge — publishable after fixing a few factual embellishments, trimming some overwriting, and tightening the ending.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'His Cameroonian heritage places him within the very geography the Tirailleurs were drawn from'
critique_issues.fix: This is accurate (Cameroon was a source of Tirailleurs), but the essay implies Ndikung's heritage gives him personal stakes in this specific history without sourcing that connection. It borders on biographical overreach. Soften to note the geographic overlap without implying personal testimony.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'Fourteen of the works are new commissions'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not specify the number of new commissions. This looks like a hallucinated specific. Remove or replace with a vaguer but honest formulation like 'multiple new commissions.'

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — Camp de Thiaroye described as 'one of the most significant African films ever made about the betrayal of colonial soldiers'
critique_issues.fix: This is defensible but grandiose. The film is significant, but 'one of the most significant African films ever made' is a big claim made casually. Specify that it's a landmark of African cinema — still strong, less sweeping.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'designed by Hugh Stubbins for the 1957 Interbau exhibition, originally a gift from the United States to West Berlin'
critique_issues.fix: The Kongresshalle was indeed designed by Stubbins and funded by the Benjamin Franklin Foundation as a US contribution to the 1957 Interbau. However, calling it 'a gift from the United States' is a simplification — it was funded by an American foundation, not the US government directly. The source material doesn't specify this detail at all; the essay is adding architectural history from general knowledge, which is fine, but should be precise. Add a confidence marker here.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — David Olusoga described as having 'done more than almost anyone's to bring colonial military service into mainstream Anglophone consciousness'
critique_issues.fix: Superlative claim. Olusoga is prominent but this is unprovable. Tone down to 'whose work has been central to bringing...'

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'Abel Selaocoe performing with Bantu Ensemble'
critique_issues.fix: Not mentioned in the source material — the source only names Cheikh Lô by name in the concert listings. This could be accurate from other promotional materials, but flag with a confidence marker or soften.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1 — 'Not forgot — that implies an accident. This was something more deliberate'
critique_issues.fix: This is a strong rhetorical move but it's also a well-worn one (the 'not X — Y' correction device). It works here because the content earns it. Keep but be aware the device shows up again later; don't overuse it.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'This is not an opening where you look at art, drink wine, and leave.'
critique_issues.fix: Slightly too pleased with itself. The sentence is doing the thing where the writer flatters the event's ambition rather than interrogating it. Cut or reframe.

'whose work on Germany's colonial afterlives is meticulous and unsettling, brings a specifically German perspective to a history that Germany has largely treated as someone else's problem' — this is good but could be sharper. Name a specific work or approach. As written, it's a vague endorsement.

This paragraph is too long and reads as a curated list with commentary bolted on. The Tiffany Chung detail is genuinely interesting and does argumentative work (widening the frame beyond France). The rest risks becoming a catalogue. Trim the Attia and Ntjam descriptions to make room for the ideas to breathe.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'The architecture was built as propaganda; the exhibition turns it into a site of counter-memory.'
critique_issues.fix: 'Counter-memory' is academic jargon. It's earned here given the context, but 'site of counter-memory' is a phrase that has appeared in a thousand exhibition catalogues. Rephrase.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — 'the difference between an important exhibition and a transformative one'
critique_issues.fix: This is the kind of sentence that sounds wise but says nothing actionable. It's a critic's hedge dressed up as a conclusion. Either commit to a prediction or cut it.

The ending is strong — the 'advance guard' etymology is genuinely good and the final sentence lands. But the paragraph takes too long to get there. The first two sentences repeat the density-of-programming point already made. Cut the throat-clearing and go straight to the argument.
'Ndikung and co-curator Paz Guevara' — Paz Guevara appears once and then vanishes. Either give them real presence in the essay or don't name them. As-is, it reads like a press release credit.

Not that there are many others like it. “The Haus der Kulturen der Welt is completely unique”, Silvia Fehrmann, the institution’s former Head of Communications, claimed to me. “Berlin is unlike any other city. Because of its divided history, it has two or even three main theatres, two zoos, and so on…” [...] Risin
